title: Reading a requirement and asking clarifying questions
objectives: Read a Salesforce requirement as an incomplete brief: outcome, users, objects, and acceptance evidence still to be named.
Ask clarifying questions that separate business need from a requested click-path, field, or Flow.
Distinguish a well-defined requirement from a user story and from a solution already baked into the request.
Stop a mock-interview build until volume, security, exceptions, and success checks are explicit.
diagnostic_question: A hiring manager says 'We need a checkbox so reps cannot close a deal without legal review.' Before you name a field, validation rule, or Flow, which clarifying questions would you ask, and what evidence would change the design?
definition: Reading a requirement and asking clarifying questions is elicitation: drawing forth the business outcome, users, constraints, and acceptance evidence before configuring Salesforce. Trailhead's Business Analyst role page describes elicitation as asking questions to understand project goals and what stakeholders want to accomplish, then documenting those needs clearly. ([Salesforce BA role](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-business-analyst-quick-look/learn-about-the-salesforce-business-analyst-role); [Information discovery](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/business-analyst_skills-strategies/explore-techniques--information-discovery))
why_it_matters: Interviewers fail candidates who jump to a checkbox, validation rule, or Flow from a one-sentence ask. The same sentence can mean a legal hold, an approval process, a status value, or a report. Clarifying questions protect security, automation, and scope; they are not delay tactics.
sixty_second_explanation: Treat a requirement like a flight clearance, not a destination already filed. You do not take off because someone said 'add a checkbox.' You confirm who is flying, what weather (volume and exceptions), how much fuel (security and data), and what counts as a landing (acceptance). Elicitation is the preflight: interviews, observation, and document analysis until the stated need matches the intended outcome.
deeper_explanation: The Salesforce Business Analyst orientation describes elicitation as asking lots of questions to understand goals, interviewing stakeholders, researching related processes, and observing teams at work. That is the same skill an admin or developer uses in a requirements interview even without a BA title. ([Salesforce BA role](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-business-analyst-quick-look/learn-about-the-salesforce-business-analyst-role))

Trailhead's information-discovery unit groups elicitation techniques: interviews, observation, document analysis, workshops, surveys, prototyping, and process modeling. You choose the technique from the gap, not from habit. Confirm elicitation results so the stated requirement matches stakeholder intent. ([Information discovery](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/business-analyst_skills-strategies/explore-techniques--information-discovery))

Cert Prep for Business Analyst asks you to distinguish requirements from user stories so both business and technical stakeholders can engage. A requirement states a need and constraint; a user story packages who, what, and why for delivery. Neither is a Salesforce object name. ([Review Requirements](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-business-analyst-certification-prep/review-requirements); [Business Analyst credential](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/en/credentials/businessanalyst))

Well-defined requirements are version-controlled and prioritized; pain points and dependencies belong in the same conversation. Jumping to change sets or a field is a later step. ([Review Requirements](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-business-analyst-certification-prep/review-requirements))

Needs versus wants versus expectations is a scope split from Trailhead's Gather Requirements unit: needs are essential, wants are negotiable, expectations are how value is supposed to appear. Interview answers should name which bucket the ask sits in. ([Gather Requirements](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/best-practices-for-project-management/gather-requirements))

mental_model.analogy: A flight-clearance briefing: destination, weather, fuel, passengers, and a defined landing—not a passenger shouting 'just take off.'
useful_mapping: stated request → the passenger's destination shout
clarifying questions → weather, fuel, passenger, and runway checks
users and volume → passengers and payload
acceptance criteria → what counts as a landing
user story → a flight strip for one delivery slice
Salesforce field or Flow → the aircraft you choose after clearance, not before
where_it_breaks: Interviews are not FAA operations; you can ship a thin slice after enough clearance, not after infinite briefings.
A one-person team still needs the questions written down; there is no tower controller unless you name one.
A requested checkbox can be the right aircraft—after you confirm it is a need, not a want dressed as a need.
Elicitation does not replace org edition, license, or security design; those are later CAREER and SEC topics.

teach_back_prompt: Take the sentence 'Add a checkbox so deals cannot close without legal.' Ask five clarifying questions, map each to need/want/expectation, then say which Salesforce tool you still refuse to name until one answer arrives.

review_schedule.prompt: From memory, restate the core terms and one clarifying question you would ask.
Classify four realistic interview signals using this topic's decision table.
Teach the analogy, then name two places it breaks.
Walk one troubleshooting symptom from evidence to next action.
Give a two-minute interview answer without notes, then one follow-up.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: I do not design a checkbox from a one-line ask. I elicit outcome, users, volume, security, exceptions, and what 'done' looks like. A requirement is not a user story and not a Salesforce field name.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I treat the sentence as elicitation input. I ask who is blocked today, what happens on the happy path versus legal exception, who must see the record, and how we will know it worked in UAT. I separate needs from wants. Only then do I mention a field, validation rule, approval, or Flow. If the interviewer already named a checkbox, I still challenge whether that is the need or a solution.

terminology.plain: Pulling the real need out of people and documents.
terminology.precise: Drawing forth or receiving information from stakeholders; Trailhead lists interviews, observation, workshops, and related techniques in prepare, conduct, and confirm stages.
terminology.example: Interviewing a legal lead about when a deal must freeze, then confirming the notes with sales ops.
terminology.non_example: Opening Object Manager and adding a checkbox because the ticket title said Legal_Hold__c.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Requirements workshop: one elicitation technique, not the whole practice.
terminology.boundary: This lesson is the interview skill; BA certification exam tactics are only orientation.

terminology.plain: A question that removes a fork in the design.
terminology.precise: A targeted question that tests outcome, users, constraints, exceptions, or acceptance evidence before a Salesforce tool is chosen.
terminology.example: Who is allowed to close the Opportunity after legal rejects, and is that a user, a profile, or a partner community user?
terminology.non_example: Would you like a checkbox or a picklist? — that is a solution menu, not a clarifying question.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Diagnostic question: a teaching prompt in this handbook, not a stakeholder interview question.
terminology.boundary: Stop after enough evidence to choose a tool; do not interview forever.

terminology.plain: A stated need with constraints, not a field API name.
terminology.precise: A well-defined need that can be verified and prioritized; Trailhead contrasts it with a user story used to engage business and technical stakeholders.
terminology.example: Legal must review Opportunities over 250,000 USD before Stage equals Closed Won, with an audit trail of the decision.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: User story: a delivery slice (who/what/why), not the full requirement set.
terminology.boundary: Platform limits and edition gates are not invented here; mark them Needs verification.

terminology.plain: A small who-what-why card for a slice of work.
terminology.precise: A delivery-oriented statement used with stakeholders; distinct from the underlying requirement, per Trailhead Cert Prep.
terminology.example: As a sales ops analyst, I need a visible legal status on Opportunity so I can stop Closed Won until review finishes.
terminology.non_example: The entire CPQ replacement program written as one story.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Epic: a larger theme that stories sit under, not this lesson's unit of elicitation.
terminology.boundary: Story points and sprint math are neighboring agile practice, not Salesforce product behavior.

terminology.plain: How we will know the requirement is met.
terminology.precise: Observable checks agreed with stakeholders—UAT cases, reports, or audit fields—not 'it feels right.'
terminology.example: A synthetic LAB_ Opportunity at 300,000 USD cannot reach Closed Won until a LAB_ Legal user records Approve.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Definition of done for a sprint team: related, but may include code-review items this lesson does not own.
terminology.boundary: Security test cases belong with sharing/FLS topics when the constraint is access.

terminology.precise: Trailhead Gather Requirements: needs are essential, wants are desired, expectations are how stakeholders see value appearing.
terminology.example: Need: freeze Closed Won. Want: a Slack ping. Expectation: legal responds the same day.
terminology.non_example: Treating a Slack notification as a need that blocks go-live.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Non-functional requirement: performance or availability—related but not the same three buckets.
terminology.boundary: Triple constraint (scope/schedule/cost) is PM framing, not a Salesforce limit table.

terminology.plain: The current friction the requirement is supposed to remove.
terminology.precise: Cert Prep lists pain points among requirement topics; you cannot design if you only heard the requested field.
terminology.example: Reps email legal in a shared inbox and still mark Closed Won.
terminology.non_example: Legal wants Salesforce because other teams have it.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Technical debt: a system constraint, not always the user's pain.
terminology.boundary: Do not invent org metrics; ask for them.

terminology.plain: The tool the requester already named.
terminology.precise: A field, Flow, or app mentioned in the ask; it must be challenged against the outcome.
terminology.example: Please add a checkbox called Legal_OK.
terminology.non_example: Please stop incorrect Closed Won — a need without a tool.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Preferred vendor: a commercial constraint, not a Salesforce metadata type.
terminology.boundary: After clearance, the stated solution may still win.

mechanics.after: Interview, observation, or document review selected
mechanics.failure: Sending a 40-question survey for a one-field ask

mechanics.transition: Confirm need vs want vs expectation
mechanics.observe: Stakeholder agrees the freeze is a need and Slack is a want

mechanics.after: UAT cases and then field/Flow/approval options
mechanics.observe: Two synthetic scenarios that would fail today
mechanics.failure: Skipping evidence and opening Flow Builder

when_to_use: When a mock-interview requirement is a one-liner and you must show clarifying questions before naming a field.
When a stakeholder already specified a checkbox, validation rule, or Flow and you need to test whether that is the need.
When you must separate a requirement from a user story in a BA-style or admin interview.
When volume, sharing, exceptions, or legal holds are missing from the asking and you would otherwise guess.
When reading a ticket that mixes pain points with a stated Salesforce object name.
when_not_to_use: Do not use endless clarifying questions to avoid answering after outcome, users, and acceptance are already explicit.
Do not treat this elicitation lesson as a substitute for Flow vs Apex product choice once the requirement is clear.
Do not quote unofficial exam dumps while reading a requirement; use official Trailhead credential pages.
Do not skip security clarifying questions and then claim sharing was out of scope because the ask was 'just a field.'
Do not run this discovery against production customer data or real legal matters in a playground exercise.
configuration_or_code_location: Stakeholder interview notes and a version-controlled requirements list (not Setup first)
Trailhead: Business Analyst Quick Look and information-discovery module
Trailhead credential: Salesforce Certified Business Analyst
Only after clearance: Object Manager, validation rules, Flow, or approval processes in a sandbox

worked_example.scenario: In a mock interview, sales ops says: 'Add a checkbox so reps cannot close a deal without legal review.' The org already has Opportunity.StageName and a custom Legal_Queue__c public group. You have five minutes to show how you read the requirement and what clarifying questions you ask before any metadata change.
inputs: Existing Opportunity object and a legal public group
Unknown: amount threshold, who can override, partner users, time SLA

decisions.decision: Treat the checkbox as a stated solution, not the requirement.
decisions.because: The need is to stop Closed Won without legal review; the control might be a status, approval, or validation against a related Legal_Review__c record.
decisions.rejected: Creating Legal_Reviewed__c in the playground during the interview

decisions.decision: Ask threshold, actors, exceptions, and acceptance evidence before naming a tool.
decisions.because: A 10 USD deal and a 2 million USD deal, plus partner community users, change sharing and automation.
decisions.rejected: Assuming every Opportunity needs the same legal hold

configuration_or_code: Do not configure yet. Write five questions: amount threshold; who records approve/reject; Closed Lost vs Closed Won; FLS for the legal fields; UAT evidence.
Draft a requirement: Opportunities over a stated amount cannot enter Closed Won until a named legal actor records a decision, with an audit field.
Offer two tool options only after questions: validation rule plus status field, versus an approval process, versus a related Legal_Review__c object if history matters.
worked_example.output: A written requirement, a need/want split (Slack ping is a want), and two UAT cases—not a deployed checkbox.
verification: A teammate can restate the outcome without saying 'checkbox.'
Two synthetic LAB_ Opportunities (under and over threshold) are named as tests.
Security question about who sees legal comments is on the list.
worked_example.self_explanation: The candidate earned credit by reading the requirement as incomplete, asking clarifying questions, and refusing to build the stated checkbox until acceptance evidence existed.

hands_on_lab.environment: Trailhead Playground or Developer Edition with synthetic LAB_ data only. No production org.
starting_state_checks: You can create a LAB_ Opportunity in Lightning
You will not deploy to a customer production org
steps: Write the one-line ask at the top of a notes file: Add a checkbox so reps cannot close without legal.
List eight clarifying questions covering users, threshold, exceptions, sharing, audit, SLA, override, and UAT.
Mark each answer you do not have as unknown; do not invent a USD amount.
Rewrite the ask as a requirement and as one user story; keep the checkbox out of the requirement sentence.
Only if a mentor supplies answers, sketch two tool options and which UAT record would fail today.
guided_completion: Read your requirement aloud without using the word checkbox.
Name one want you would defer.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Swap the ask to 'We need a Flow that emails legal.' Repeat the same clarifying questions and show you still challenge the stated Flow.
evidence: Notes file with eight questions and a requirement sentence that names outcome not metadata.
A need/want/expectation split with at least one item in each bucket.
stop_recovery_cleanup: Delete any LAB_ fields you created if you skipped ahead to Setup.
hands_on_lab.limitations: Playground UI labels vary by release. Do not quote exam weights from memory.

decision_table.signal: Interviewer names a checkbox, validation rule, or Flow in the first sentence
decision_table.choose: Challenge the stated solution; ask outcome and acceptance first
decision_table.not: Build the named metadata during the interview
decision_table.why: Trailhead treats elicitation as clarifying goals, not implementing the first tool named

decision_table.signal: You cannot tell who uses the record or who must not see legal comments
decision_table.choose: Ask users, volume, and sharing before any field
decision_table.why: Security clarifying questions change object choice and FLS

decision_table.signal: The ask mixes a pain point with a full program ('replace CPQ this quarter')
decision_table.choose: Split needs from wants and write a thin requirement slice
decision_table.not: Treat the program as one user story
decision_table.why: Gather Requirements separates essential needs from negotiable wants

decision_table.signal: Outcome, threshold, actors, and two UAT cases are already written
decision_table.choose: Stop asking; propose field vs approval vs related object with reasons
decision_table.why: Confirm elicitation, then design; endless questions look like avoidance

decision_table.signal: Stakeholder says 'just like last org' with no current-state notes
decision_table.choose: Elicit current Salesforce usage and pain points in this org
decision_table.not: Copy the previous org's checkbox set
decision_table.why: Customer discovery includes how this customer uses Salesforce today

limitations: Elicitation skill is not a Salesforce Setup feature and has no edition toggle.
BA credential exam weights change; reverify the official page.
A clarifying question cannot discover license limits you must still look up in Help.
security_notes: Ask who must not see the data before you add a field to a page layout.
Do not use real customer legal documents in a playground lab.
Partner and Experience Cloud users are a different user population than internal reps.
common_mistakes: Building the requested checkbox in the first two minutes.
Asking only UI questions ('checkbox or picklist?').
Skipping sharing, FLS, and exception paths.
Calling a program-sized ask a single user story.
Inventing a dollar threshold instead of marking it unknown.

troubleshooting.symptom: Interviewer says you jumped to configuration
check: Did you ask who and who-not?
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: They wanted you to open Setup immediately

troubleshooting.symptom: Stakeholder answers 'just make it like Salesforce standard'
check: Which object and which standard field?
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: Standard Opportunity already enforces legal review

production_notes: Version-control the requirement list; do not leave it in chat history only.
Sandbox configuration happens after clearance, not during the first elicitation meeting.
If legal data is involved, involve security review before any production field.

mcqs.prompt: In Trailhead's BA orientation, what is elicitation primarily for?

options.A: Asking questions to understand goals and what stakeholders want to accomplish

mcqs.rationale: The BA role page frames elicitation as clarifying project goals and stakeholder intent.

distractor_explanations.B: Tool choice comes after a well-defined requirement.
distractor_explanations.C: OWD is a sharing setting, not elicitation.
distractor_explanations.D: Deployment is a later ALM step.

mcqs.prompt: Which statement best matches a well-defined requirement versus a user story?

options.A: A requirement states a verifiable need; a user story packages a delivery slice for stakeholders
options.B: They are identical Salesforce metadata types
options.C: A user story is always an Apex class name

mcqs.rationale: Cert Prep asks you to distinguish requirements from user stories and to keep requirements in a version-controlled repository.

mcqs.prompt: A ticket says 'Add Legal_Reviewed__c.' What is the best first clarifying question?

options.A: What business outcome fails today if legal has not reviewed, and how will we observe success?
options.B: Should the checkbox be on the page layout or the Lightning record page?
options.C: What API version should the field use?
options.D: Which change-set name do you prefer?

mcqs.rationale: Challenge the stated field; recover outcome and acceptance evidence.

distractor_explanations.B: Layout is a later presentation choice.
distractor_explanations.C: Fields do not pick Apex API versions like classes.

mcqs.prompt: Which bucket is 'legal must block Closed Won on large deals' if go-live is otherwise unsafe?
mcqs.rationale: Needs are essential functions that must be included for the deliverable to work.

distractor_explanations.D: Story points are not the need/want split.

mcqs.prompt: You still do not know whether Experience Cloud partners close Opportunities. What should you do?

options.A: Ask who the users are and who must not see legal comments before proposing a field
options.C: Hide the field with CSS in LWC
options.D: Skip sharing because it is an interview

mcqs.rationale: Users and sharing are clarifying questions that change the design.

mcqs.prompt: Outcome, actors, threshold, and two UAT cases are already on the whiteboard. Next best move?

options.A: Propose two Salesforce options and a recommendation with trade-offs
options.B: Ask twenty more open questions to appear thorough
options.C: Refuse to design until a BA is hired

mcqs.rationale: Confirm elicitation, then design. Endless questions look like avoidance.

distractor_explanations.D: Never use production for the exercise.

options.A: Reps still mark Closed Won while emailing legal versus 'add a checkbox'
options.C: Pain point is always a custom object
options.D: Stated solution is always the requirement

mcqs.rationale: Pain is current friction; the checkbox is a proposed control.

distractor_explanations.C: Pain is not an object type.
distractor_explanations.D: The stated solution must be challenged.

mcqs.prompt: Which elicitation technique fits 'I need to see how reps actually close from the list view'?

options.D: Skipping elicitation and writing a trigger

mcqs.rationale: Trailhead lists observation among elicitation techniques when the work is in people's hands.

distractor_explanations.C: Prototyping is another technique, not the first here.

mcqs.prompt: What does the Business Analyst credential page say certified BAs do?

options.A: Understand business needs, capture requirements, and collaborate on Salesforce solutions
options.C: Set MFA for the whole industry
options.D: Replace sharing rules with page layouts

mcqs.rationale: The official credential page uses that collaboration framing.

mcqs.prompt: Which note is acceptance evidence for the legal-review requirement?

options.A: A LAB_ Opportunity over the agreed amount cannot reach Closed Won until a legal user records Approve
options.D: The checkbox is on the layout

mcqs.rationale: Acceptance is an observable business check, not a deploy log.

distractor_explanations.D: Layout visibility is not the freeze.

mcqs.prompt: Stakeholder: 'Make it exactly like our last Salesforce org.' Best clarifying move?

options.A: Discover how this org uses Salesforce today, including pain points and constraints
options.B: Copy every field from memory of the last org
options.C: Install an unmanaged package of the old org

mcqs.rationale: Customer discovery includes current-state Salesforce usage; copying blindly skips elicitation.

distractor_explanations.B: Orgs differ by edition, licenses, and process.

mcqs.prompt: You are asked to 'just confirm the requirement is a checkbox.' How do you keep reading the requirement?

options.A: Restate the business freeze, then ask whether a status, approval, or related record would also meet it
options.B: Agree immediately to end the meeting
options.D: Move the field to a different object at random

mcqs.rationale: Keep challenging stated solutions against the outcome.

distractor_explanations.C: API names are not the requirement.
distractor_explanations.D: Random object moves are design without evidence.

flashcards.front: What is elicitation on the Salesforce BA Trailhead pages?
flashcards.back: Drawing forth goals and needs from stakeholders through interviews, observation, research, and related techniques.

flashcards.front: Requirement vs user story in one sentence?
flashcards.back: A requirement is a verifiable need; a user story is a delivery slice that helps business and technical people engage.

flashcards.front: First move when the ask names a checkbox?
flashcards.back: Treat it as a stated solution. Ask outcome, users, exceptions, and acceptance before Object Manager.
Need is essential scope; want is negotiable; expectation is how value is supposed to feel or appear.

flashcards.front: Name two clarifying questions for 'cannot close without legal.'
flashcards.back: What amount or record type is in scope, and who is allowed to override a legal reject?

flashcards.front: What is acceptance evidence for that legal freeze?
flashcards.back: A synthetic over-threshold Opportunity cannot become Closed Won until a named legal actor records a decision.

flashcards.front: When is observation the right elicitation technique?
flashcards.back: When the gap is how people actually work in Salesforce, not what they say they do.

flashcards.front: Prepare, conduct, confirm — what is confirm?
flashcards.back: Validate that stated requirements match stakeholder intent before you build.

flashcards.front: Is a clarifying question the same as a solution menu?
flashcards.back: No. 'Checkbox or picklist?' is a tool menu. 'What fails in the business today?' is clarifying.

flashcards.front: Which clarifying question is a security question?
flashcards.back: Who must not see legal comments, including partners or other roles?

flashcards.front: What does the Business Analyst credential emphasize?
flashcards.back: Understanding needs, capturing requirements, and collaborating on Salesforce solutions.

flashcards.front: What happens if wants are treated as needs?
flashcards.back: Scope inflates; schedule and cost move. Slack pings should not block a legal freeze.

flashcards.front: When should you stop asking clarifying questions in an interview?
flashcards.back: When outcome, users, constraints, and two test cases are explicit enough to compare tools.

flashcards.front: Is documenting a requirement a metadata change?
flashcards.back: No. The requirement list is an analysis artifact. Fields and Flow are metadata after clearance.

flashcards.front: Why is 'just like the last org' a weak requirement?
flashcards.back: It skips current-state discovery for this org's licenses, process, and pain points.

flashcards.front: Write a user story that does not name a checkbox.
flashcards.back: As sales ops, I need Closed Won blocked until legal records a decision so we do not book unreviewed revenue.

interview_questions.question: How do you read a one-line Salesforce requirement in an interview?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I treat it as incomplete. I extract outcome, users, constraints, and acceptance before any object or Flow name.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I say the sentence is elicitation input, not a build ticket. I list unknowns: who, volume, exceptions, security, and how we will test. I distinguish the stated tool from the need. I will not invent a dollar threshold. Then I offer a requirement sentence the interviewer can correct.
interview_questions.example: Add a checkbox so reps cannot close without legal — rewritten as a freeze on Closed Won with an audit decision.
tradeoffs: Speed of sounding decisive vs accuracy
Challenging the interviewer vs seeming obstructive
follow_ups: What if they insist on the checkbox?
How many questions is too many?
weak_answer_warnings: Opening Object Manager in the first minute

interview_questions.question: What is elicitation, and which techniques would you actually use?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Elicitation is drawing needs from people and documents. I pick interviews, observation, workshops, or document review based on the gap.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Trailhead lists many techniques; I do not recite them as a laundry list. For a legal-close rule I interview legal and sales ops, glance at current Opportunity layouts, and confirm notes. A 40-question survey is the wrong instrument. I confirm results so the written requirement matches intent.
interview_questions.example: Watching a rep close from the Opportunity list view because email-to-legal is invisible in Setup.
weak_answer_warnings: Listing BABOK terms with no Salesforce example

interview_questions.question: The interviewer already wants a checkbox. How do you ask clarifying questions without looking difficult?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I restate the outcome I heard, then ask one constraint question and one acceptance question, offering to use a checkbox if it still fits.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I credit their solution: a checkbox might be right. I ask what Closed Won means in the business, who records legal's decision, and how we demo success. If they confirm a simple boolean with FLS for legal, I take the checkbox. If they need history, I float a related record. I never mock the ask.
interview_questions.example: Legal_Reviewed__c with FLS versus a Legal_Review__c object after they mention multiple review cycles.
tradeoffs: Simple field vs auditable related object
follow_ups: What if they say there is no legal user in Salesforce?

interview_questions.question: You are given a requirement that mixes a Slack notification, a legal freeze, and a CPQ replacement. What do you do?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I split need, want, and expectation, and I refuse to treat the program as one user story.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I name the legal freeze as a need if booking unreviewed revenue is the risk. Slack is a want. CPQ replacement is a different initiative. I write one requirement and one story for the freeze, with two UAT Opportunities. I say scope, schedule, and cost will move if we keep everything as needs.
interview_questions.example: Go-live on the freeze with a report; Slack and CPQ on a later roadmap.
tradeoffs: Thin slice vs political pressure to keep everything
follow_ups: How do you say no to a VP?
Where do you write this down?
weak_answer_warnings: Calling the whole program a single story

interview_questions.question: Halfway through, you realize you never asked who can see legal comments. Recover.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I name the miss, ask the sharing question now, and say it can change object and FLS choices.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I do not pretend I asked it. I say security was an unknown. I ask about internal roles, executives, and Experience Cloud partners. If partners close deals, a field on Opportunity with wide OWD is the wrong shape. I update the requirement and the UAT users. Interviewers score the recovery.
interview_questions.example: Partner Community users who currently have Opportunity access would see a legal comment field unless sharing and FLS change.
tradeoffs: Field on Opportunity vs private child object
follow_ups: When do you bring an architect?
weak_answer_warnings: Saying security is out of scope

interview_questions.question: The stakeholder cannot articulate the requirement. How do you still make progress?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I switch technique: observe the current close path, inspect a redacted sample, or walk a failed report, then confirm.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Interviews fail when people cannot name the need. Trailhead includes observation and document analysis. I ask to see the last deal that should have been blocked. I write a draft requirement and read it back. If they only have feelings, I still will not invent a threshold; I mark it unknown.
interview_questions.example: A last-quarter Closed Won that legal later reversed, used as a concrete pain point.
follow_ups: What if they refuse to show data?

interview_questions.question: After clarifying questions, how do you choose between a validation rule, an approval process, and a related object?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I match the now-clear constraints: simple block, routed decision with history, or many reviews over time.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Once outcome and actors are known, tool choice is AUTO-001 territory, but I still show judgment. A same-record boolean with a validation rule can freeze Closed Won. Approvals fit a named legal queue. A child Legal_Review__c fits multiple cycles. I do not pick Apex for a same-record freeze Flow or validation can cover. I state edition and license as Needs verification if asked for exact gates.
interview_questions.example: Validation rule on Stage plus a status field after they said one legal approver and no history UI needed.
tradeoffs: Declarative freeze vs auditable child object
follow_ups: When would Flow beat a validation rule?
Where does this sit versus AUTO-001?

interview_questions.question: Teach reading a requirement without jargon to a sales VP.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I will not build the first button you name. I will ask what 'done' looks like, who is in the plane, and what weather we cannot fly in.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use the flight-clearance analogy: destination is the business outcome, passengers are users, restricted airspace is sharing, landing is a test we can watch. A checkbox is an airplane type. I say where it breaks: we can still ship a thin slice; we will not brief forever. I invite the VP to correct the destination sentence.
interview_questions.example: VP said checkbox; you wrote 'stop booking unreviewed revenue' and asked for a sample deal.
follow_ups: How do you document this for IT?
